title: Apache Kafka and event streaming architecture
description: In-Sync Replicas (ISR), High Watermark, KRaft consensus, idempotent producer deduplication, and sticky rebalances.

questions.text: In an Apache Kafka topic with replication factor 3 and min.insync.replicas=2, how does a producer with acks=all behave?

options.text: The write succeeds only if all 3 replicas acknowledge receipt
The write succeeds as long as at least 2 in-sync replicas (including the leader) acknowledge receipt; if only 1 replica is in-sync, writes are rejected with NotEnoughReplicasException
The write is acknowledged immediately by the leader without waiting for followers
The write is stored in OS page cache on the leader and flushed to disk asynchronously

questions.explanation: With `acks=all`, the leader waits for all current in-sync replicas to acknowledge. If follower crashes drop the ISR size below `min.insync.replicas` (2), the broker rejects further writes to guarantee durability against leader crashes.

questions.text: What is the difference between a partition's Log End Offset (LEO) and its High Watermark (HW)?

options.text: LEO is the offset of the next record to be written by the leader; High Watermark is the highest offset replicated across all in-sync replicas and visible to consumers
High Watermark is the next record written; LEO is the consumer offset
LEO is only tracked on followers; High Watermark is only tracked on the controller
There is no difference; they are aliases for the same offset integer

questions.explanation: LEO represents the end of the leader's local append-only log. The High Watermark (HW) lags behind LEO until followers catch up; consumers are strictly forbidden from reading past the High Watermark to prevent dirty reads if an un-replicated leader crashes.

questions.text: How does Kafka's Idempotent Producer guarantee exactly-once message delivery per partition without duplicate records?

options.text: By calculating an MD5 hash of the payload and storing it in Redis
The broker assigns a unique Producer ID (PID); each message carries a monotonically increasing Sequence Number that the broker deduplicates
By executing a Two-Phase Commit transaction with all active consumers
By delaying message acknowledgment by 5 seconds to detect duplicates

questions.explanation: With `enable.idempotence=true`, the broker assigns a 64-bit Producer ID (PID). For each partition, the producer tags records with consecutive sequence numbers ($0, 1, 2, \dots$). If a network retry occurs, the broker recognizes that sequence number $K$ was already committed and ignores the duplicate.

questions.text: What major architectural improvement does the KRaft (Kafka Raft) metadata mode introduce over the legacy ZooKeeper architecture?

options.text: It eliminates the external ZooKeeper cluster, running Raft-based metadata consensus directly inside Kafka brokers for instantaneous metadata failover and support for millions of partitions
It compresses message payloads with Zstandard by default
It removes consumer groups in favor of direct socket streaming
It mandates schema validation via JSON schema

questions.explanation: KRaft stores metadata in an event-sourced, append-only metadata log managed directly by controller quorum nodes running Raft. This removes the ZooKeeper synchronization bottleneck, enabling rapid controller elections and scaling to tens of millions of partitions.

questions.text: In Kafka consumer groups, the Cooperative Sticky Assignor avoids the 'stop-the-world' pause of eager rebalancing by revoking only the specific partitions being moved.
questions.explanation: True. Eager rebalancing forces all consumers to revoke all partitions and stop processing during rebalances. Cooperative Sticky rebalancing uses a phased approach: consumers continue processing untouched partitions while only reassigned partitions are migrated.
